metadata.title: From Zero to Hero: The Hearthcross Years
metadata.systemCompatibility: 5E-compatible fantasy RPG with explicit Level-0 house rules

premise.playerPitch: You begin at twelve years old with six 9s, no class, and a whole village that still sees you as a child. Over seven years you do chores, compete at fairs, make friends, disappoint people, learn trades, leave home for the first time, survive a storm, and face the night Hearthcross finally needs you. Every win and loss becomes a scrapbook card. By the end, the scrapbook explains the Level-1 adventurer you became.
premise.gmSummary: Run one chapter per age from 12 through 18. Each chapter contains exactly three shared Growth Beats. Every player gets one Development Check in each beat before that beat closes. The player-facing Zero-to-Hero sheet owns the development wallet, Upbringing Lean, cards, Yearbook, and graduation math. This adventure owns pacing, read-aloud, NPC pressure, group choices, contest procedure, and the evolving village. Early chapters are deliberately ordinary. Serious danger begins at 17. The age-18 Watchstone crisis pays off people, places, promises, and mistakes accumulated across the earlier years.
premise.winCondition: There is no single win condition. The adventure succeeds when the four-to-six players complete all seven years, preserve their consequences, finish 21 personal Development Checks each, and graduate with a legal 27–30 Level-0 base array before entering certified 2014 or 2024 Level-1 creation.
premise.failureRule: Failure always changes the story and the scrapbook; it never removes a player's baseline development or bricks the campaign.

tableContract.spotlightRule: In every Growth Beat, every player gets one distinct Development Check before the beat closes. Rotate who acts first from beat to beat and chapter to chapter.
fourPlayerProcedure: Name Players A–D at session start.
Beat 1 starts with A, Beat 2 with B, Beat 3 with C; next chapter starts with D, then continue rotating.
After the first action changes the scene, ask the next player what they do in the new situation; do not replay the exact same check.
A character may help another in the fiction but still needs their own Development Check.

scaling.5: Add one more distinct task, witness, delivery, rival, or consequence in each Growth Beat; do not raise DCs.
scaling.6: Add two more distinct tasks or consequences and split crowded scenes into two simultaneous fronts; do not raise DCs.

rulesBoundary.level0: All developmental checks, Upbringing Lean, natural-20/natural-1 growth tiers, Lesson Points, scrapbook development cards, 27 floor, and 30 ceiling are explicit Level-0 house rules.
rulesBoundary.level1: Once the base array is frozen, 2014 or 2024 rules become authoritative for race/species, background, class, HP, proficiency, saves, spells, feats, equipment, and later advancement. Do not mix editions.
rulesBoundary.safety: Ages 12–15 use embarrassment, responsibility, cost, damaged property, strained relationships, and ordinary accidents rather than routine lethal stakes. Age 16 adds travel risk. Age 17 introduces serious danger. Age 18 contains the true origin crisis.

hearthcrossSix.purpose: A balanced six-contest slate used across childhood celebrations. One contest is keyed to each ability so every 2/2/2 Upbringing Lean encounters exactly two Favored, two Neutral, and two Challenging contests across the slate.
hearthcrossSix.ranking: For each core contest, all contestants use the named primary ability. Use the character's Upbringing Lean and Character Advantage cancellation. Rank by final check total, then kept d20, then one story-only d20 tiebreak. Placement grants a scrapbook award but no extra Development Point.

chapters.title: Spring Chore Day
chapters.sessionGoal: Make the party feel like children who belong to the same village before asking them to be heroes.
chapters.openingReadAloud: Spring has finally beaten the last gray ice out of Hearthcross. The Common Green is crowded with carts, brooms, buckets, fence rails, and adults holding lists far too long for one morning. For the first time, your names are written on the youth work board instead of beside your parents'.
dmOpening: Have each player introduce their home, one chore they hate, and one person in Hearthcross they do not want to disappoint.
Confirm each player has chosen an Upbringing Lean before the first Development Check.
Tell the players nobody is grading their acting; concrete choices and history are enough.

beats.title: The Job Board
beats.purpose: Establish teamwork and first adult trust.
beats.readAloud: Five jobs are circled in chalk: firewood, shrine steps, a broken fence, flour delivery, and medicine delivery. Wren Cask folds her arms and points at the sky. “Rain by the third bell. Decide who does what before the weather decides for you.”
runSteps: Put all five jobs on the table at once.
Ask the first player to choose a responsibility and method; resolve that character's Development Check.
Change the fiction based on that result, then move to the next player with a different remaining problem.
For four players, leave one job dependent on how well the group coordinates; for five or six, each player can own a job.
beats.consequence: Record which household or institution the party prioritized. That group begins treating them as dependable—or remembers being left waiting.
beats.scrapbookPrompt: Name one object from the chore day that would still make the character remember being twelve.
beats.location: Common Green and the five work routes radiating from it. Cool spring sun, wet earth, hammering from the fence line, yeast and smoke from the bakery lane. The Watchstone stands at the north edge of the Green where all five routes remain visible.
fourPlayerJobs: Repair or brace the broken goat fence.
Move and stack the shrine firewood before rain.
Deliver flour without tearing the sacks.
Carry Maela's medicine parcel to the far cottages.

lines: Pick a job you can finish, not one you can brag about.
If you need help, ask before the fence falls over.
Rain doesn't care whose fault it is.
Why does the water groove point toward the old stone?
I'll trade you firewood duty for literally anything.
I drew your name on the work board bigger. You're welcome.

mysteryClues: If any character works near the Watchstone or crosses the Green after the first drizzle, Nima points out three shallow chevrons cut near its base. Do not explain them.
branches: If the group prioritizes Maela, she remembers it at age 15 when assigning apprentices.
If the fence is neglected, Clover's escape in the next beat starts closer to the herb beds.
beats.advanceWhen: Every player has completed one distinct responsibility and the first drops of rain begin.

beats.title: Clover Gets Loose
beats.purpose: Turn an ordinary mistake into a group comedy with real consequences.
beats.readAloud: There is a crack of wood, a delighted bleat, and Mara Hale's goat Clover shoots through the half-mended fence with six feet of rope bouncing behind her. She makes straight for Maela Venn's neat rows of spring herbs. Maela looks at you, then at the goat. “Please tell me that's still your problem.”
runSteps: Run Clover as a moving problem, not combat.
Each player's action changes Clover's position: garden, wash line, flour cart, shrine steps, then fence unless stopped earlier.
Do not end the beat after the first successful catch; later players handle damage control, frightened animals, broken fence, or Maela's reaction.
A failure creates a funny cost; a critical failure should create a memorable mishap card, not serious injury.
beats.consequence: If the garden is damaged, the group owes Maela a future favor. If it survives, she becomes an early source of trust.
beats.scrapbookPrompt: Give the goat incident a nickname the village would still use six years later.
beats.location: Mara Hale's fence line, Maela Venn's herb rows, a wash line, flour cart, and shrine steps all within a messy fifty-yard chase. The ground is damp enough to slide but not dangerous.
fourPlayerJobs: Cut Clover off before the herb rows.
Protect or repair what Clover has already hit.
Calm a second frightened animal tied near the flour cart.
Coordinate adults or children so the chase does not become worse than the goat.

lines: Clover! That is not a road!
Please catch the goat before Maela learns new words.
Nobody tells your aunt about this version of the story.
Those are feverfew seedlings.
The goat is negotiable. The seedlings are not.
If you save half the bed, I will call this educational.

mysteryClues: If Clover bolts across the Common Green, she refuses to step directly beside the Watchstone and jerks around it hard enough to drag her rope sideways.
branches: Saved herb bed: Maela owes the group a small favor later.
Damaged bed: the group helps replant between years and may gain a specific herb-garden familiarity memory.
beats.advanceWhen: Clover is contained and each player has dealt with one separate consequence of the escape.

beats.title: Rain Before Supper
beats.purpose: End the first year with responsibility instead of spectacle.
beats.readAloud: The third bell has not rung, but the rain comes anyway—fat cold drops that turn dust to dark spots in seconds. Flour, lamp oil, and medicine are still on the cart. Three households are waiting, and the road is already becoming mud.
runSteps: Put the three deliveries and worsening weather in front of the group.
Every player chooses what they protect, carry, reroute, or sacrifice.
On failure, something arrives late/wet/damaged but no household loses an essential medicine dose; fail forward.
End with the group arriving home soaked and being treated a little less like children.
beats.consequence: The village gains its first opinion of the group as a unit.
beats.scrapbookPrompt: What did the character bring home from the rain: an object, a bruise, a compliment, or an argument?
beats.location: Rain-dark village lanes between Crossmarket, the shrine, outlying cottages, and the river road. The rain is cold, wagon ruts fill quickly, and the smell of wet flour and lamp oil follows the cart.
fourPlayerJobs: Keep medicine dry and deliver it first.
Protect flour sacks from water and mud.
Get lamp oil safely down the slick lane.
Choose and communicate a route when one lane floods.

lines: Look—the puddle's going the wrong way.
No, seriously. Water does not climb hills.
I'm drawing it before it stops.
The Green drains strangely every spring. Keep moving.
Deliveries first, mysteries tomorrow.
Good work. Now get warm.

mysteryClues: At the Watchstone, rainwater runs a few feet uphill through an old groove before vanishing under the turf. Pike dismisses it as old drainage.
branches: Fast deliveries build a 'dependable' reputation.
A damaged parcel creates an owed favor or apology, not a medical tragedy.
beats.advanceWhen: The essential medicine arrives, every player has resolved a delivery/weather problem, and the group reaches home soaked.

chapters.closeReadAloud: That winter, adults still call you children—but now they sometimes call your names when work needs doing.
chapters.chapterArc: Responsibility: adults give the children real work for the first time.

chapters.title: The Spring Dance
chapters.sessionGoal: Make social victories and embarrassments as important as physical ones.
chapters.openingReadAloud: A year later, ribbons cross the Fox & Ferry yard and every window in Crossmarket has a spring lantern hanging in it. The dance does not begin until sunset, which means the village has given the youth crews all afternoon to make mistakes where everyone can see them.
dmOpening: Ask what changed about each character physically or socially since last spring.
Run the CHA Hearthcross Six contest—Lantern Presentation—as an optional placement card before Beat 1; it adds no DP by itself.
Put Kess, Nima, and one chosen family member into the evening.

beats.title: Before the Music
beats.purpose: Give the group ownership of the celebration.
beats.readAloud: Benches are in the wrong place, two lantern poles lean toward the food tables, and half the older youths have vanished the moment someone mentioned carrying barrels. The musicians are already tuning.
runSteps: Let each player claim a setup problem.
If someone won or lost the Lantern Presentation, let that result color how villagers react to them.
Resolve all players before the music begins.
Use success to improve the party's position in Beat 3; use failure for running jokes and repair work.
beats.consequence: A clean setup earns public praise; a messy one creates a village story that can return in later dances.
beats.scrapbookPrompt: What decoration, ribbon, lantern, or mistake becomes the image the character remembers?
beats.location: Fox & Ferry yard and Common Green before sunset. Fresh-cut ribbons snap overhead, bread and onions roast near the inn, musicians tune under an awning, and unfinished lantern poles lean at worrying angles.
fourPlayerJobs: Brace and align a lantern pole.
Rearrange benches so older villagers have clear access.
Recover missing barrels or serving ware.
Organize younger helpers abandoned by older teens.

lines: The dance starts when the musicians do, not when we're ready.
If that pole falls, aim it away from the pies.
You lot wanted to be treated older. Congratulations.
Mine is straighter than yours.
Winner gets first pick of the sweet buns.
Don't look at the knot. The knot is temporary.

mysteryClues: Old Sable watches the Watchstone rather than the decorations. If approached she asks, 'Does it always hum before rain here?' even though the sky is clear.
branches: Clean setup gives the group easier crowd cooperation in dance-3.
Visible mistakes become named scrapbook jokes that NPCs may repeat years later.
beats.advanceWhen: The yard is safe enough for the musicians to begin and all players have solved one setup problem.

beats.title: The Awkward Middle
beats.purpose: Let relationships create mechanical history without forcing romance.
beats.readAloud: The first hour goes well enough that people begin making bad social decisions. Someone has been left out, Kess is showing off, a friend has heard a rumor that may not be true, and somebody is pretending not to care who asked whom to dance.
runSteps: Ask each player which social problem they notice or choose to ignore.
No romance is mandatory; friendship, rivalry, family embarrassment, and loyalty are equally valid.
A player can earn Character Advantage by invoking a real relationship or prior memory.
Failure strains a relationship; it never forces a romantic outcome.
beats.consequence: Update one friend/rival/mentor relationship per character.
beats.scrapbookPrompt: Who did the character spend time with when nobody was assigning them a job?
beats.location: The dance in full swing: packed earth underfoot, lantern smoke and fried apples in the air, music loud enough that private conversations require stepping to the yard edge.
fourPlayerJobs: Notice and include someone being left out.
Address a rumor involving a friend or family member.
Deal with Kess or another rival showing off at someone's expense.
Choose whether to tell a difficult truth or protect someone from embarrassment.

lines: You can tell me if you don't want to dance. That's easier than pretending.
Kess heard the rumor too.
Do you ever think about leaving Hearthcross?
I was joking. Mostly.
Don't make that face like you're better than me.
Fine. I shouldn't have said it where everyone could hear.

mysteryClues: If anyone steps near the Watchstone during a quiet moment, the hum disappears under a hand placed on the stone, then returns when they let go.
branches: Reconciliation can turn a rival into support later.
Public humiliation can harden a rivalry but must never force romance or attraction.
beats.advanceWhen: Each player has made one relationship-defining choice and the musicians announce the final set.

beats.title: Lanterns in the Wind
beats.purpose: Give the chapter a group-action finish while keeping stakes ordinary.
beats.readAloud: A gust runs through the yard hard enough to make every flame lean sideways. One lantern line tears free, then a second. A pole starts to fall toward the crowded food tables while the musicians keep playing because nobody has told them to stop.
runSteps: Give every player a distinct front: falling pole, loose line, hot lantern, crowded table, frightened younger child, or keeping the dance calm.
If the group resolves things cleanly, the music never stops.
On failure, move the dance indoors or lose food/decorations; nobody is seriously injured.
End with one last-song choice.
beats.consequence: The last-song choice becomes a Yearbook relationship memory.
beats.scrapbookPrompt: What part of this embarrassment or triumph gets retold next spring?
beats.location: Fox & Ferry yard during a sudden crosswind. Lantern lines whip overhead, one pole tips toward the food tables, and the crowd compresses toward the inn doors.
fourPlayerJobs: Catch or redirect the falling pole.
Pull a loose lantern line away from people and cloth awnings.
Move children or elders out of the crush.
Keep the crowd calm and the musicians informed.

lines: Watch the flames, not the wind.
There. They bend toward the stone.
Still drawing breath, then.

mysteryClues: Several lantern flames point toward the Watchstone even after the wind shifts the opposite direction. Sable's comment is the first explicit hint that she recognizes the behavior.
branches: If the dance continues outside, villagers remember the group saved the celebration.
If moved inside, the final song becomes more intimate and changes which relationships get spotlighted.
beats.advanceWhen: The lantern hazard is contained, everyone is safe, and the group chooses where the final song happens.

chapters.closeReadAloud: The last song ends, lantern smoke hangs in the rafters, and the walk home feels shorter than it did last year.
chapters.chapterArc: Belonging: the characters decide who they are among peers when nobody assigns them a role.

chapters.title: Harvest Fair & Team Games
chapters.sessionGoal: Make winning and losing visible, fair, funny, and formative.
chapters.openingReadAloud: Harvest banners turn Crossmarket gold and red. This year your names are not just on the work board—they are on the competition slate. Ribbons, wooden trophies, and one extremely suspicious pie crown wait on the judges' table.
dmOpening: This is the best chapter for the Hearthcross Six. Run as many placement contests as the table enjoys; use the three Growth Beats for the major fair situations.
Across the six core contests, each Upbringing Lean gets exactly 2 Favored, 2 Neutral, and 2 Challenging lanes.
Every player gets a placement card in every contest they enter.

beats.title: Pick Your Event
beats.purpose: Let competition identity emerge without letting one stat dominate the whole fair.
beats.readAloud: A bell rings and six chalkboards flip over: Sack Haul, Rat Race, Pie Eating, Riddle Table, Scavenger Hunt, Lantern Presentation. Kess grins across the green. “Pick carefully. I plan to remember this forever.”
runSteps: Run at least two Hearthcross Six contests now, preferably one physical and one mental/social.
For each contest, everyone who enters uses the same primary ability; record official placement 1st through field size.
Award 1st/2nd/3rd podium cards and unique consolation/mishap cards to everyone else.
The Growth Beat Development Check remains the player's broader response to competition—training, pressure, sportsmanship, strategy, nerves, or recovery—not an extra placement DP.
beats.consequence: Establish who is competitive, gracious, resentful, fearless, or unexpectedly talented.
beats.scrapbookPrompt: Which ribbon, trophy, joke award, or failure goes in the scrapbook?
beats.location: The Common Green transformed into six contest lanes with chalkboards, rope barriers, ribbons, judges' stools, and a long prize table. Bells, cheering, dust, berry pie, and livestock noise overlap.
fourPlayerJobs: Enter or help run one physical contest.
Enter or help run one mental/perceptive contest.
Handle a rival challenge or sportsmanship moment.
Record or dispute a placement without derailing the fair.

lines: Pick your event. I plan to remember this forever.
If you beat me, I will deny it by winter.
If I beat you, I expect dramatic suffering.
Totals first, kept die second, and if you still tie I get the joy of making you roll again.
Third place is a podium. Do not let first place propaganda tell you otherwise.
Everybody gets a card. Some cards are kinder than others.

mysteryClues: The WIS Scavenger Hunt's final clue leads to the north edge of Alderwood where a buried marker bears the same three-chevron symbol Nima drew at age 12.
branches: A character who wins gracefully earns different reputation than one who gloats.
A consolation card can become as socially memorable as a podium card.
beats.advanceWhen: At least two core contests have been run, every participating player has an official result card, and each player has resolved the Growth Beat.

beats.title: The Stall Rush
beats.purpose: Remind players the fair is also family work.
beats.readAloud: The fair reaches its loudest hour at exactly the wrong moment. A pie tray tips, two family stalls are short-handed, and a merchant's mule plants all four feet in the middle of the lane. Somewhere behind you, a judge is calling the next event.
runSteps: Force a choice between competition glory and helping people.
Every player gets a separate practical problem.
Character Advantage should often come from family duties, earlier chores, or a relationship.
On failure, money, food, or pride is lost—not campaign access.
beats.consequence: Families remember whether the character showed up when fun competed with responsibility.
beats.scrapbookPrompt: What did the character miss—or give up—to help?
beats.location: Crossmarket at peak fair hour. Family stalls crowd the lane, a mule blocks the center, hot pies slide on uneven boards, and contest bells keep calling competitors away.
fourPlayerJobs: Help a family stall during a rush.
Control or reroute the stubborn mule.
Save a dropped or tipping tray without injuring anyone.
Choose between making the next contest call and keeping a promise to help.

lines: The fair can survive one blocked lane.
No, the mule does not need an official permit.
Please stop asking whether the standing stone is part of the scavenger hunt.

mysteryClues: If the market lane is cleared, a wheel briefly drops into a shallow depression above the buried east conduit. Wren remarks that the ground should not be hollow there.
branches: Skipping an event to help family creates a bond/reputation memory.
Choosing the contest instead is allowed; the family consequence should be personal, not moralized by the DM.
beats.advanceWhen: The lane functions again and every player has chosen what mattered more to them in the rush.

beats.title: The Final Relay
beats.purpose: End the fair on teamwork rather than individual ranking.
beats.readAloud: The closing relay is deliberately unfair: a carry, a balance beam, a memory station, an animal gate, and a crowd-facing finish. The judges do not care who has the best single talent. They care whether your team gets everybody across.
runSteps: Give each player a different relay job aligned with the fiction they choose.
Do not allow one high roll to carry the whole team; each player resolves once.
Failure changes final placing but the team finishes together.
If you want one more Hearthcross Six result, run the remaining core contest after the relay as an epilogue.
beats.consequence: The group's reaction to winning or losing becomes village reputation.
beats.scrapbookPrompt: What did the team do immediately after the result was announced?
beats.location: A relay course looping around the Green: weighted carry, balance beam, memory station, animal gate, and a raised finish platform facing the whole fair.
fourPlayerJobs: Handle the carry or physical obstacle.
Take the balance/precision segment.
Solve or remember the station clue.
Manage the animal gate or crowd-facing finish.

lines: Do not drop the token. I drew the clue on it.
We finish together or Kess will be unbearable.
After this, come see what we found in the woods.

mysteryClues: After the relay, Nima can show the group her age-12 sketch beside the newly found Alderwood marker. The three-chevron marks match closely enough to be deliberate.
branches: Team placing affects reputation but not development budget.
If the party dismisses the symbols, Nima continues keeping the evidence anyway.
beats.advanceWhen: Every player completes a different relay segment and the team crosses the finish together.

chapters.closeReadAloud: By sunset the ribbons matter less than the stories. Some people won. Some lost. Everybody remembers exactly who laughed, who sulked, and who stayed to help clean up.
chapters.chapterArc: Competition: winning and losing become public memories without defining worth.

chapters.title: Apprentice Week
chapters.sessionGoal: Let characters discover work, mentors, and identities without granting premature proficiency.
chapters.openingReadAloud: At fifteen, adults stop asking what games you like and start asking what work you can do. For one week every youth in Hearthcross rotates through real jobs before choosing where to spend more of the coming year.
dmOpening: Offer at least four mentor stations relevant to the party: Orren, Sera, Elwen, Bram, Tavi, Maela, Wren, or Jory.
Make clear that familiarity is story/history only until a legal Level-1 source grants proficiency.
Ask each player what they hope they are good at—and what they fear they are not.

beats.title: Morning Rotations
beats.purpose: Test assumptions about what each child thinks they will become.
beats.readAloud: The first bell sends everyone in a different direction: forge smoke, herb steam, ink, animals, customers, drills, ledgers. By midday, every one of you has discovered at least one job that looks easier from across the street.
runSteps: Give each player a mentor and concrete task.
Success earns praise but not proficiency.
Failure should teach technique, patience, humility, or a different ability lane.
Record one mentor quote suitable for a scrapbook memory card.
beats.consequence: A mentor may offer future time based on attitude, not just success.
beats.scrapbookPrompt: What did the mentor say that the character still remembers at eighteen?
beats.location: A rotating circuit through forge, remedies shop, records room, shrine yard, training yard, bee sheds, and inn. Each place smells and sounds completely different; the characters are old enough to be trusted with real tools but not unsupervised mastery.
fourPlayerJobs: Complete a careful physical/craft task.
Handle a customer or community request.
Research, copy, or sort records accurately.
Work with an animal, patient, trainee, or younger helper.

lines: Copy what is there, not what you think should be there.
That mark again. I have seen it in an older ledger.
No, you may not take the brittle page outside.
Good work is the part nobody notices later.
If the old wood lies to you, believe the sag, not the paint.
Measure twice is advice for optimists. Measure three times.

mysteryClues: Sera shows a partial copied diagram with three lines radiating from a central stone, but the labels are missing. She has not yet connected it to the village map.
branches: Mentors offer future time based on attitude and accountability, not only success.
Failure can redirect who the character enjoys learning from.
beats.advanceWhen: Each player completes a mentor task and names one thing they want to learn more—or less—about.

beats.title: The Crooked Pavilion
beats.purpose: Make the party solve an adult problem together.
beats.readAloud: Halfway through repairing the market pavilion, Wren stops the work with one raised hand. The old support beneath your new boards is crooked—badly crooked—and fixing only what you were assigned would hide the problem for another year.
runSteps: Present the choice: finish on time with the hidden flaw or admit the larger repair.
Every player's check addresses a different part of the correction or negotiation.
Failure costs materials/time; critical failure means redoing work and facing embarrassment.
The pavilion's eventual condition should remain visible in later chapters.
beats.consequence: The group learns whether professional responsibility matters more than looking competent.
beats.scrapbookPrompt: Did the character sign the hidden repair beam? Why or why not?
beats.location: The Crossmarket pavilion, half stripped for repairs. Sawdust floats in sunlight, old posts smell of rot, and one support hides a gap beneath newer boards.
fourPlayerJobs: Brace the pavilion safely while the support is exposed.
Determine how much old material must actually come out.
Explain the larger problem to Pike or merchants who want the market reopened.
Trace the unexpected stonework beneath the post without destabilizing it.

lines: This isn't a bad board. It's a bad answer built over an older question.
There is dressed stone under my post.
Reeve, someone cut a channel through here before there was a pavilion.
Cover it safely. I will request an inspection.
No digging under the market without authority.
We have stalls to reopen tomorrow.

mysteryClues: The repair exposes the east conduit: fitted stone, a shallow groove, and the same keeper mark. Pike's reaction suggests this is not the first report he has seen.
branches: Insist on documenting it: Sera gets a rubbing and future Advantage evidence.
Accept Pike's order quietly: the conduit is re-covered, making age-17 access harder but not impossible.
beats.advanceWhen: The pavilion is structurally safe and the group decides whether the old channel gets documented before it is covered.

beats.title: A Real Customer
beats.purpose: Introduce professional responsibility and fairness.
beats.readAloud: A traveler limps into the work yard with a damaged cart, a cut hand, a missing delivery paper, and not enough coin to solve all four problems. Your mentors do not answer for you. They wait to see what you do.
runSteps: Let each player take one aspect of the customer's problem.
Do not make charity automatically correct; fair trade, clever substitution, or calling in a favor are valid.
Failure may cost the mentor money or time and requires repair/accountability.
If helped well, the traveler becomes a later Bellmere contact.
beats.consequence: The party gains or loses one outside contact before age 16.
beats.scrapbookPrompt: What did the customer leave behind: thanks, debt, advice, complaint, or small object?
beats.location: Wren and Maela's shared work yard at late afternoon. A traveler's damaged cart leans on one wheel, blood dots a wrapped palm, and the delivery papers are rain-softened.
fourPlayerJobs: Stabilize or repair the cart.
Treat or comfort the injured traveler within ordinary first-aid limits.
Resolve the missing/unclear paperwork.
Find a fair way to cover the work when the traveler cannot pay for everything.

lines: I can pay for the wheel or the hand, not both.
Bellmere clerks love paper more than people.
If you ever come through the east gate, ask for Iven Dorr. I owe Hearthcross.

mysteryClues: If helped well, Iven mentions Bellmere road archives contain old district surveys whenever a village disputes buried infrastructure.
branches: Help creates a Bellmere contact for age 16.
Exploit or dismiss him means the party must navigate Bellmere archives without that shortcut.
beats.advanceWhen: The traveler can safely leave and every player has owned one part of the problem.

chapters.closeReadAloud: By the end of the week, your hands know things they did not know on Monday. None of it makes you an adventurer yet. It does make adults start asking when you can work again.
chapters.chapterArc: Craft and accountability: doing adult work means admitting when the problem is larger than your assignment.

chapters.title: The Road to Bellmere
chapters.sessionGoal: Make independence feel exciting before making it dangerous.
chapters.openingReadAloud: At sixteen, the village gives you something it has never given you before: a cart, a delivery list, and no adult sitting beside you. Bellmere is only a day away. That feels very far when Hearthcross disappears behind the trees.
dmOpening: Ask who each family warned before departure.
Let the party choose who holds the money, map, animal lead, and letters.
Use the outside contact from Apprentice Week if one exists.

beats.title: Packing the Cart
beats.purpose: Let planning and interpersonal conflict happen before the road.
beats.readAloud: There is more cargo than cart. Flour cannot get wet, medicine cannot freeze, lamp oil should not sit beside either, and three families have quietly added packages that were not on the original list.
runSteps: Force priorities rather than inventory trivia.
Every player owns one load/route/social problem.
Failure creates a later inconvenience, not a dead end.
Record who accepted responsibility for the purse and paperwork.
beats.consequence: How they pack changes the ford or market complications.
beats.scrapbookPrompt: What did someone secretly pack from home?
beats.location: Hearthcross cart shed at dawn. Flour, medicine, lamp oil, letters, personal parcels, blankets, feed, and too many family requests compete for a finite wagon bed.
fourPlayerJobs: Prioritize and secure cargo.
Check route, weather, and timing.
Manage the horse and harness.
Negotiate which unofficial parcels can come.

lines: River's high but falling. Probably.
If the horse refuses a crossing, assume she noticed something before you did.
Bellmere is one day away if nothing interesting happens.

mysteryClues: Sera slips the party a copied three-line Watchstone diagram and asks them to look for any matching survey notation in Bellmere if they get the chance.
branches: Well-packed cargo reduces consequences at Alder Ford.
Taking too many favors creates social obligations in Bellmere but can also earn contacts.
beats.advanceWhen: The cart is loaded, four core responsibilities are assigned, and the party leaves Hearthcross without an adult escort.

beats.title: Night at Alder Ford
beats.purpose: Give the first unsupervised risk without turning it into combat.
beats.readAloud: The river is higher than Bram predicted. The usual stones are underwater, dusk is close, and the cart horse has decided the rushing water is a terrible idea. Hearthcross is behind you. Bellmere is ahead. Nobody older is coming to decide.
runSteps: Let the group choose cross now, find another way, or camp.
Every player resolves a different aspect: depth, animal, rigging, cold water, shelter, negotiation with a nearby farmer.
Failure costs time, wet supplies, or repair; do not sweep anyone away to death.
Make the second night away possible if they lose too much time.
beats.consequence: Family trust at home later depends on honesty about what happened.
beats.scrapbookPrompt: What did the character hear in the dark that made home feel far away?
beats.location: Alder Ford at dusk. Brown water covers the normal stepping stones, reeds hiss in wind, horse breath steams, and the nearest farmhouse light is a quarter mile away.
fourPlayerJobs: Judge the river and choose whether to cross.
Calm and manage the horse.
Rig cargo or shelter against water/weather.
Negotiate shelter/help or find a safer alternate route.

npcDialogue.voice: If traveling with the party, exhilarated and nervous
lines: This is officially farther than I've ever been without family.
I vote we don't drown for the sake of being on time.
Look at the stones on the north bank. Same cutting style as the marker.

mysteryClues: A dressed stone on the north bank uses the same old construction style as the Alderwood marker, suggesting the pre-village builders worked beyond Hearthcross too.
branches: Cross now risks wet cargo but saves time.
Camp costs time but can protect goods.
Ask the farmer for help creates a new regional relationship.
beats.advanceWhen: The party has a safe plan for the night/ford and every player resolves a different travel responsibility.

beats.title: Bellmere Market
beats.purpose: Show a world where nobody knows the children's reputations.
beats.readAloud: Bellmere does not care who your parents are. One customer has moved, one merchant disputes the written price, and the market bell says you have less than an hour before stalls close.
runSteps: Give each player one unfamiliar-city problem.
Use documentation, observation, negotiation, endurance, speed, or labor as appropriate.
Failure can cost money or an extra night; all required deliveries still have a fail-forward route.
Let one outsider treat a character according to what they actually did, not what Hearthcross thinks of them.
beats.consequence: Each character records whether leaving home feels more or less attractive now.
beats.scrapbookPrompt: What small Bellmere souvenir proves the trip happened?
beats.location: Bellmere market and district records office. Stone paving, shouting vendors, horse dung, spice smoke, and clerks behind a brass-railed counter make Hearthcross feel very small.
fourPlayerJobs: Complete a disputed delivery.
Find a moved customer or correct address.
Negotiate an incorrect price or missing receipt.
Get access to the old district survey before the records office closes.

lines: Hearthcross. Old road district, north shelf.
You want drainage, boundary, or pre-charter stonework? Those are different ledgers.
Do not fold the survey. I will know.
You made it. Good. Tell Ada I sent you.
I said I owed Hearthcross, not that I enjoy the clerk's office.
Take a copy. Old roads cause new arguments every year.

mysteryClues: The survey labels the Watchstone a 'relief cap' and shows three arms. A margin note reads: 'Keep all three relief ways open after flood or road work.' Part of the south route is missing from the damaged sheet.
branches: Acquire a copy: major age-18 Advantage evidence.
Only memorize it: Sera can reconstruct most of it later, but exact routing is harder.
Miss the office: Iven can mail a copy later if he is an ally.
beats.advanceWhen: The required deliveries are complete and the party either obtains, memorizes, or loses access to the survey evidence.

chapters.closeReadAloud: The road back into Hearthcross looks smaller than the road out did. People ask how it went. For the first time, you get to decide which version of the story they hear.
chapters.chapterArc: Independence: the characters learn what changes when nobody older is there to decide.

chapters.title: The Long Storm
chapters.sessionGoal: Introduce serious stakes while proving the previous five years mattered.
chapters.openingReadAloud: The storm begins with warm rain and no wind. By noon, the Hearth River is brown and fast. By afternoon, the watch bell rings twice—the signal for every able hand to report. This time, nobody sends you home.
dmOpening: Bring back consequences: repaired pavilion, Maela's garden/shop, family stalls, Bellmere road, mentor health.
Tell players the village cannot save everything; people take priority over property.
Serious injury is possible now, but failure still moves forward.

beats.title: Before the River Rises
beats.purpose: Turn six years of familiarity into preparation choices.
beats.readAloud: Boards, sandbags, animals, children, ledgers, medicine, grain—everyone is shouting a different priority. Orren points at your group instead of assigning you one task. “You know this village. Decide where you're useful.”
runSteps: Offer at least six tasks tied to recurring locations.
Each player chooses one and resolves once.
Use old scrapbook memories to justify Character Advantage where specific.
Failure makes a later crisis worse rather than injuring someone immediately.
beats.consequence: Mark one location as well-prepared and one as underprepared if the group cannot cover everything.
beats.scrapbookPrompt: Which adult looked at the character differently after this?
beats.location: Hearthcross under relentless warm rain. Sandbag lines cross the Green, animals crowd covered yards, river noise carries through every street, and the Watchstone gives off a barely audible vibration.
fourPlayerJobs: Protect homes/shops on low ground.
Move medicine, food, or records to higher storage.
Secure animals and dangerous loose materials.
Inspect known Watchstone/conduit sites using earlier clues.

lines: You know this village. Pick where you're useful.
People first. Buildings second. Pride nowhere.
If you see the old stone move, tell Sera before you tell the crowd.
The Bellmere drawing fits the market channel.
If there are three arms, one of them is under this water.
I need observations, not theories.

mysteryClues: The Watchstone hum and water behavior now clearly match the Bellmere survey. The south spill is not relieving pressure as it should.
branches: Prior preparation from ages 12–16 can save a location automatically from property damage but never erase another player's Growth Check.
Ignoring the old conduits makes storm-3 worse.
beats.advanceWhen: Every player has secured one priority and the river rises high enough to trigger the missing-person alarm.

beats.title: Someone Is Still Out There
beats.purpose: Deliver the first real rescue.
beats.readAloud: A riderless cart horse comes back through the rain with one rein torn loose. At almost the same moment, a family realizes an older relative never came home. The road noise is so loud you have to shout to hear each other.
runSteps: Choose missing NPCs from the relationship list when possible.
Every player contributes to finding, reaching, stabilizing, transporting, or coordinating.
A failed first route makes the rescue harder; it does not erase the person.
A critical failure can cause a scar, lost keepsake, or relationship consequence.
beats.consequence: The rescued person's later graduation reaction depends on this scene.
beats.scrapbookPrompt: What did the character lose or damage during the rescue?
beats.location: Outer road, flooded pasture, and drainage ditches in driving rain. Visibility drops to fifty feet; a riderless cart horse returns with torn tack.
fourPlayerJobs: Track or infer the missing person's route.
Cross or bypass a flooded obstacle.
Stabilize the missing NPC once found.
Coordinate transport back through worsening weather.

lines: Horse came back from the old road, not the river path.
Water erases tracks. Broken grass doesn't.
Bring them home. Then we can argue about why they were out there.

mysteryClues: Near the old road, floodwater disappears abruptly into a collapsed stone-lined cut—the east relief arm—with fresh rubble from Rusk's side passage.
branches: If Rusk is trusted or redeemed, he admits the smuggling cut and shows a safer entrance.
If hostile, the party can still find the passage from physical evidence.
beats.advanceWhen: The missing person is recovered and the party has seen enough of the east-arm damage to report it.

beats.title: One Crew, Two Crises
beats.purpose: Force an adult-scale priority decision.
beats.readAloud: The mill wall groans. Across the lane, water punches through the doors of three homes. You have enough people to guarantee one problem and only maybe enough to save both.
runSteps: State clearly: lives can be saved in either plan, but property/location outcomes differ.
Let the group split if desired; keep spotlight moving between fronts.
Every player resolves one check; accumulated results determine how much property survives.
Do not invent a perfect no-cost answer unless earned by exceptional play.
beats.consequence: Permanently alter at least one Hearthcross location.
beats.scrapbookPrompt: What choice does the character still defend—or regret—at eighteen?
beats.location: Crossmarket and the low residential lane as two crises unfold: the mill wall groans under water pressure while floodwater forces doors in three homes. The Watchstone's vibration can now be felt through the soles of boots.
fourPlayerJobs: Lead the mill effort.
Lead the home evacuation.
Open or clear part of the market conduit.
Coordinate people/resources between the two fronts.

lines: The old reports said settling. They did not say this.
I thought opening the ground would cause panic.
If you have a better order, give it now.
Three arms. North, east, south. It isn't a ward wall—it's a relief system.
The stone is not holding something in. It is trying to let something out safely.
We have been building over the exits.

mysteryClues: This beat reveals the campaign truth: the three-arm relief system is failing. Do not reveal every final solution yet.
branches: Save mill first: homes are evacuated but property loss is worse.
Save homes first: mill damage affects next year's economy.
Split efficiently: both can survive partially, but one conduit-access route is lost.
beats.advanceWhen: Lives are safe, at least one property consequence is locked in, and Sera publicly explains the three-arm theory.

chapters.closeReadAloud: When the water drops, Hearthcross is still standing. It is not unchanged. Neither are you.
chapters.chapterArc: Duty: the village needs them during real danger and cannot save everything.

chapters.title: The Last Spring Dance
chapters.sessionGoal: Pay off the entire scrapbook and hand the characters into Level 1.
chapters.openingReadAloud: Six years after your first spring dance, younger children are hanging lanterns badly in all the familiar ways. Some of you may leave after tonight. Some may stay. Everyone in Hearthcross seems to know that, even when nobody says it.
dmOpening: Before play, review each character's scrapbook and choose one family member, one friend/rival, and one mentor to feature.
Bring back at least three physical village consequences from earlier chapters.
The Watchstone crisis is not a monster fight by default; it is a community problem whose solution depends on what these characters learned.

beats.title: This Time, You're in Charge
beats.purpose: Mirror age 13 and show the characters have become the older youths.
beats.readAloud: A younger helper knots the lantern line wrong. Another stacks benches where the musicians need to stand. Five years ago, adults fixed your mistakes. Tonight, everybody looks at you.
runSteps: Give each player a younger helper who resembles one of their own old mistakes.
Resolve teaching, delegating, correcting, or quietly redoing.
Success creates a legacy; failure shows what the character still has not learned.
Keep the scene affectionate rather than punitive.
beats.consequence: Each player gains one nonmechanical 'Someone Looked Up to Me' or equivalent memory card.
beats.scrapbookPrompt: What mistake did the character recognize because they once made it?
beats.location: Common Green on the afternoon of the final Spring Dance. Younger teens repeat all the old mistakes: crooked lanterns, misplaced benches, tangled ribbons. The characters now stand on the adult side of the work list.
fourPlayerJobs: Teach a younger helper instead of taking over.
Correct a safety problem without humiliating anyone.
Delegate a task to someone unreliable or nervous.
Decide how much of last year's Watchstone concern to mention during preparations.

lines: Look at them. We were never that bad.
Do not answer that.
One last contest before everyone becomes unbearable adults?

mysteryClues: The Watchstone has a hairline crack exactly along one branch of the three-chevron mark. Sera has been checking it all winter.
branches: Patient teaching creates a younger ally during the finale.
Taking over everything gets tasks done faster but leaves younger helpers less useful later.
beats.advanceWhen: The dance grounds are ready, every player has handed responsibility to someone younger, and sunset begins.

beats.title: The Last Song Before Midnight
beats.purpose: Resolve unfinished relationships before the crisis.
beats.readAloud: The music slows. There are people you may not see every week after tonight: family, rivals, mentors, friends, maybe someone you hurt or never thanked. Midnight is close enough that everyone is suddenly brave or suddenly quiet.
runSteps: Give every player one chosen conversation.
Character Advantage should frequently come from Yearbook memories and relationship cards.
Do not force reconciliation; clarity is a valid success.
Failure means the truth comes out badly, not that the relationship becomes impossible forever.
beats.consequence: Freeze the relationship state that enters Level 1.
beats.scrapbookPrompt: What words does the character wish they had said differently—or is glad they finally said?
beats.location: The edge of the dance under steady lantern light. Familiar songs, familiar smells, and people who may not all be together next spring create a quiet pocket before midnight.
fourPlayerJobs: Speak with a family member about leaving or staying.
Resolve or redefine the Kess rivalry.
Ask a mentor what adulthood changes between them.
Tell Nima/Rusk/Pike/Sable something left unsaid.

lines: You found the pattern without me. Good.
My family called themselves keepers. Mostly that meant remembering what needed doing.
I will tell you what I know. I will not choose what Hearthcross becomes.
I kept every sketch.
The crack matches the first drawing from when we were twelve.
Whatever happens after tonight, don't pretend none of this mattered.

mysteryClues: If the party has connected at least three earlier clues, Sable reveals her keeper ancestry and confirms the system's purpose. If not, she still gives enough truth to prevent a dead end, but the party loses an easy Character Advantage justification.
branches: Relationships resolve according to accumulated history; no reconciliation is mandatory.
Sable becomes an advisor, never the decision-maker.
beats.advanceWhen: Each player has one final relationship conversation and the midnight bell begins.

beats.title: When the Watchstone Rings
beats.purpose: Make the final crisis a synthesis of six years of growth.
beats.readAloud: At midnight the Watchstone rings like a struck bell, though nobody touched it. A black crack races down its face. The Common Green shudders, old stone channels split open beneath the grass, and every lantern flame bends toward the standing stone at once.
runSteps: Reveal that the Watchstone is an old pressure-and-ward structure, not a boss monster.

Give six simultaneous jobs: brace the exposed channel, evacuate the green, interpret Sera's copied ward marks, read the tremor pattern, carry the keystone, and unite frightened adults behind one plan.
For four players, combine jobs but keep four distinct checks; for five or six, use one job each.
Use relevant mentors/locations/cards as Advantage hooks.
Failure should destroy or scar a meaningful village location, relationship, or heirloom path; Hearthcross survives through a costly second route.
After every player acts, let the group choose whether to restore the old ward, safely vent/break it, or preserve part of it for future study.
beats.consequence: The chosen resolution becomes the first adult reputation of the party and the final Hearthcross state carried into Level 1.
beats.scrapbookPrompt: What single object from the green goes into the scrapbook as the last Level-0 card?
beats.location: Common Green at midnight. The Watchstone cracks with a bell-like report; turf splits along three buried lines; dust rises from Crossmarket; river water shivers against the current; every lantern flame bends inward.
fourPlayerJobs: Stabilize or move the exposed capstone/keystone.
Evacuate and organize the Green.
Interpret diagram, sketches, and survey evidence.
Open or reroute one blocked relief arm while directing villagers.

lines: North, east, south—pick what we're doing and I can tell you where.
Do not patch the crack until we know where the pressure goes.
This is infrastructure. Treat it like infrastructure.
Tell me what stays and what breaks.
I can move stone. I cannot move indecision.
If we sacrifice the pavilion, say it now.
Restore it, open it, remake it. All three are choices.
The old keepers made theirs.
Now Hearthcross makes yours.

mysteryClues: The final geometry confirms all earlier evidence. Players should be able to point to scrapbook memories that justify at least one useful action.
branches: Restore: clear three arms and reseat the old capstone; ongoing keeper duty becomes a village institution.
Vent: deliberately ruin the regulating throat and permanently reshape the Common Green into an open spill channel.
Retune: sacrifice/rebuild one affected structure and create a new balanced routing using current knowledge.
beats.advanceWhen: All players complete their final Development Check, the group chooses one of the three infrastructure resolutions (or a clearly equivalent player-created solution), immediate danger ends, and the village witnesses the result.

chapters.closeReadAloud: Dawn comes over a Hearthcross that knows your names for reasons that have nothing to do with your parents. Whatever you become next, nobody here can honestly call you children anymore.
graduationProcedure: Resolve all remaining Lesson Points and Maturity Settlement on each player sheet.
Confirm every base array is at least 27 and no more than 30 point-buy value.
Choose 2014 or 2024 separately for each character only if the campaign allows mixed player editions; never mix mechanics inside one character.
Print the Coming-of-Age Certificate, Origin Chronicle, and scrapbook cards.
Only then begin certified Level-1 character creation.
chapters.chapterArc: Adulthood: relationships resolve, the childhood mystery becomes a civic crisis, and the group chooses what Hearthcross carries forward.

gmAuditChecklist: Every player resolved exactly three Development Checks per chapter.
No Growth Beat ended before all players acted.
No early chapter used lethal combat as the default stake.
Upbringing Lean changed odds but never changed the starting six 9s.
Character Advantage was based on specific fiction, not acting skill.
Competition placement never awarded extra Development Points.
All scrapbook Development Cards reconcile with the player sheet.
The final Level-0 array is 27–30 and no score exceeded 15 before edition-specific Level-1 adjustments.
2014/2024 mechanics begin only after the Level-0 array is frozen.

campaignMystery.name: The Watchstone Breathes
campaignMystery.dmTruth: The Watchstone is not a prison and there is no monster sealed beneath Hearthcross. It is the visible capstone of an old three-channel relief system built before the village to bleed dangerous magical-geological resonance out of a deep spring and stone fault. The north arm vents through a buried stone circle in Alderwood, the east arm runs beneath Crossmarket and the old pavilion toward the road, and the south arm spills pressure toward the Hearth River. Generations of repairs, roadwork, forgotten maps, and one smuggler-cut side passage have narrowed or blocked all three. The system has been warning the village for years. The age-17 storm cracks the already stressed matrix; the following spring thaw pushes it to failure during the age-18 dance.
campaignMystery.theme: The mystery is about inherited responsibility, not defeating evil. Adults forgot, hid, misunderstood, or postponed maintenance. The children become the generation that finally sees the whole pattern.
campaignMystery.noVillainRule: Do not reveal a mastermind. Reeve Pike hid reports because he feared panic and economic damage. Rusk's smuggling worsened one channel but did not create the problem. Old Sable looks suspicious because she knows too much, but she is trying to discover whether Hearthcross can become its own keeper again.

threeReliefArms.name: Alderwood Vent
threeReliefArms.route: Watchstone → buried stone circle north of town
threeReliefArms.problem: Tree roots and a collapsed capstone constrict the old vent.
threeReliefArms.keyEvidence: Three clues: Clover refuses to pass beside the Watchstone (age 12); the age-14 scavenger hunt exposes a matching keeper mark in Alderwood; the dressed stone at Alder Ford (age 16) matches it.

threeReliefArms.name: Market Conduit
threeReliefArms.route: Watchstone → beneath Crossmarket pavilion → old road
threeReliefArms.problem: Successive repairs covered access points; smugglers later cut a side passage that filled part of the conduit with rubble.
threeReliefArms.keyEvidence: Three clues: a cart wheel drops into the hollow lane above the conduit (age 14); the crooked pavilion repair exposes marked stonework (age 15); floodwater vanishes into the collapsed cut beside Rusk's side passage (age 17). By age 17 Rusk knows the side passage.

threeReliefArms.name: River Spill
threeReliefArms.route: Watchstone → Fox & Ferry lane → Hearth River
threeReliefArms.problem: Silt, flood repairs, and a newer retaining wall choke the spillway.
threeReliefArms.keyEvidence: Three clues: age-12 rain runs uphill toward the stone; the Bellmere survey is missing part of the south route (age 16); age-17 floodwater surges backward through the old drain.

clueLadder.clue: During the rain, water briefly runs uphill through a shallow groove toward the Watchstone. Nima sketches three nested chevrons on the stone before the puddle hides them again.
clueLadder.meaningLater: The first visible sign of the three-channel system.

clueLadder.clue: When the lantern lines snap, several flames bend toward the Watchstone even after the wind changes. Old Sable quietly says, 'Still drawing breath, then.'
clueLadder.meaningNow: Sable is odd and the stone is stranger than adults admit.
clueLadder.meaningLater: The relief system is pulling energy toward the capstone.

clueLadder.clue: The scavenger hunt uncovers a weathered north marker bearing the same three-chevron keeper mark. Bram notes that deer refuse to cross the nearby ring of stones.
clueLadder.meaningNow: A fair clue leads somewhere unexpectedly old.
clueLadder.meaningLater: This is the north relief arm.

clueLadder.clue: Removing the crooked pavilion brace exposes dressed stone below the market with a channel groove and keeper mark. Pike orders it covered until 'someone qualified' can inspect it.
clueLadder.meaningLater: This is the east conduit and evidence that Pike has seen reports before.

clueLadder.clue: A Bellmere survey copy labels Hearthcross's old standing stone as a 'relief cap' and warns that three drains must remain open. The document is incomplete but unmistakable.
clueLadder.meaningNow: Proof that the Watchstone once had a practical function.
clueLadder.meaningLater: The characters can identify the three arms before the final crisis.

clueLadder.clue: Stormwater bursts backward from the market drain while the Watchstone hums hard enough to rattle cups. Sera overlays the party's clues and finally sees the three-arm diagram.
clueLadder.meaningNow: The forgotten system is failing now.
clueLadder.meaningLater: The party knows what must be inspected over winter.

clueLadder.clue: The crack in the Watchstone follows the same three-chevron geometry from the childhood clues. The crisis is the accumulated maintenance failure becoming visible all at once.
clueLadder.meaningLater: The final choice determines how Hearthcross handles inherited responsibility going forward.

finaleOptions.name: Restore the Old Relief System
finaleOptions.requirements: Use Sable/Sera's keeper knowledge, expose all three arms, clear the blockages, and reseat the capstone.
finaleOptions.cost: Hearthcross keeps the Watchstone and accepts an ongoing keeper/maintenance duty.
finaleOptions.future: The village preserves the old system but can no longer pretend it is self-maintaining.

finaleOptions.name: Open the System Permanently
finaleOptions.requirements: Break the old regulating throat in a controlled way and route the stored pressure through the south spillway.
finaleOptions.cost: The Watchstone is ruined and part of the Common Green becomes a permanent stone-and-water channel.
finaleOptions.future: The old ward no longer needs keepers, but Hearthcross visibly changes.

finaleOptions.name: Build a New Three-Arm Balance
finaleOptions.requirements: Combine Sera's diagram, Bellmere survey knowledge, Wren's structural skill, and player-devised routing to rebalance the arms.
finaleOptions.cost: Requires sacrificing or rebuilding one earlier village structure selected from the campaign's consequences.
finaleOptions.future: Hearthcross keeps a functioning system that belongs to the current generation rather than copying the old one exactly.

recurringArcs.start: Same-age rival who needs to be first at something.
recurringArcs.middle: The Harvest Fair determines whether rivalry becomes mutual respect, resentment, or friendship.
recurringArcs.late: During the Long Storm, Kess volunteers before being asked. She can become a reliable second crew leader if the characters ever treated her as more than competition.
recurringArcs.age18: At the Last Spring Dance she either jokes about old defeats, demands one final contest, or quietly admits she is afraid everyone will leave.

recurringArcs.start: Friend and sketcher who notices patterns adults ignore.
recurringArcs.middle: Her drawings become the most consistent visual record of changes around the Watchstone.
recurringArcs.late: She returns from time away with a Bellmere drawing technique that helps compare old marks precisely.
recurringArcs.age18: Her childhood sketches can supply Character Advantage when the party identifies the three-channel crack.

recurringArcs.start: Older youth who makes shortcuts sound clever.
recurringArcs.middle: By Apprentice Week he is doing errands for smugglers using an old market-side passage.
recurringArcs.late: The smuggling passage has worsened the east conduit blockage. Rusk can confess, flee, or help clear it depending on earlier treatment.
recurringArcs.age18: He is evidence that one bad choice can matter without making him the campaign's secret villain.

recurringArcs.start: Competent village authority who values calm and reputation.
recurringArcs.middle: He repeatedly delays investigation of old Watchstone reports because each year offers a more urgent ordinary problem.
recurringArcs.late: The Long Storm proves the reports were real. He can admit the suppression or double down until confronted with the Bellmere survey.
recurringArcs.age18: He yields authority to the young adults if they have evidence and community trust; otherwise he tries to centralize the response.

recurringArcs.start: An outsider who appears to know why the standing stone matters.
recurringArcs.middle: She drops precise fragments rather than solving the mystery for the children.
recurringArcs.late: She reveals her keeper ancestry only after the party independently connects at least three clue sources.
recurringArcs.age18: She refuses to choose the finale for them: 'A keeper who chooses for the village is only another kind of lock.'
